name: Henna cones

card.summary: Ready-to-use cones of henna paste that let people stain brows, hands and skin a reddish brown for a defined, fuller look without mixing powder.
card.note: 'Black henna' cones may contain PPD, which can cause blistering, scarring and lasting allergy.

quick.overview:
Henna cones are pre-mixed paste in a piping cone, used to draw designs on skin or fill in eyebrows. The paste releases lawsone, a dye that binds to skin proteins and leaves an orange stain that darkens to reddish brown over about three days.

For appearance, brow users get a temporary stained shape that looks like filled-in brow, and body-art users get designs on hands and feet. Stains fade within one to three weeks.
quick.how: The cone tip is cut and paste is piped along the area, left on for a period, then scraped or brushed off dry because water can interfere with staining. Traditional cones are mixed fresh from powder; commercial ready-made cones are sold for convenience.
quick.risks: Natural henna paste loses staining power within about a week, so shelf-stable cones may contain other chemicals that are often undisclosed. 'Black henna' products may contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), reported to cause blistering, scarring and lifelong sensitisation, and henna poses serious risk to people with G6PD deficiency.

lead: Henna cones are conical bags of henna paste used to apply the plant dye in fine lines. Henna comes from powdered leaves of Lawsonia inermis; the paste releases lawsone, which binds to skin proteins.[1] Cones are especially associated with India, while Moroccan applicators more often use syringes.[1]

In appearance use, henna paste stains skin orange, darkening to reddish brown over roughly three days and fading within one to three weeks.[1] It has been used as a temporary substitute for eyebrow pencil and in henna brow shaping.[1] Ready-made cones appeal because they skip mixing, but the Wikipedia henna article notes that fresh natural paste is not shelf-stable and that long-lasting commercial cones likely contain other, often undisclosed, ingredients.[1]

chain: Paste is piped onto brows or skin
Lawsone dye binds to skin proteins
A reddish-brown stain defines the brow or design for one to three weeks
angle.text: Cones let people draw a stain onto brows to look fuller and more defined, or decorate hands and feet. The stain appears orange and deepens over about three days.

paras: Henna has been used since antiquity across North Africa and the Middle East for hair, skin and nails, and spread to South Asia and other regions.[1] Whole leaves do not stain; dried leaves are milled into powder and mixed with liquids such as water, lemon juice or tea, then rested before use.[1] The cone is the common applicator in India.[1]

Applied to the face, henna is used as a temporary alternative to brow pencil.[1] Practitioners usually remove dried paste by scraping or brushing rather than water, which can interfere with the stain.[1]

The Wikipedia article states that natural paste loses its ability to stain within about a week, so commercial cones that stay effective longer probably contain other chemicals such as sodium picramate, which are often undisclosed, and many are still marketed as natural.[1]

'Black henna' often contains no henna. It may be indigo or para-phenylenediamine (PPD); PPD can cause blistering, intense itching, scarring and lifelong sensitisation, with reactions often appearing 3 to 12 days later.[1] Warning signs listed include a paste that darkens skin within about 30 minutes.[1] Black henna pastes may contain 10 to 80 percent PPD, versus under 6 percent in hair dyes.[1] Henna also poses serious risk to people with G6PD deficiency.[1]

The US FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application; it is permitted only as a hair dye, and imports for body art can be seized.[1] PPD is prohibited for skin use in Western countries, though enforcement is difficult.[1]

timeline.event: Henna used in North Africa and the Middle East for hair, skin, nails.[1]
Pre-Raphaelite circles popularise henna-dyed hair in Europe.[1]
